name: shapes/canonical-form-and-id
about: A shape's id is the hash of its canonical text, and that id is an identity the protocol leans on: it is what a trusted-shape allowlist admits, what a client sends instead of the text, and what a cached result is keyed by. Two implementations that canonicalise differently do not disagree loudly - they simply stop recognising each other's shapes.
source: spec 02 §3, which gives the sorting and the separators; spec 12 §4.2 for the number form inside an argument. The canonical text of every case below was written from those rules by hand, and each id is the SHA-256 of that text taken with a general-purpose digest - not read out of a Rayfold runtime. The runtime is what is being checked.
rule: Expand named-view spreads; type-condition spreads stay.

Sort items at each level by kind - fields, then '...on', then '@defer', then named-view spreads - and within a kind: fields by output name (the alias when there is one) then canonical args, type conditions by type name, defers by label, spreads by Type.view.
Sort arguments by name. Values are canonical JSON, numbers included; a $name reference is kept verbatim.
Items of a shape and arguments of a field are separated by one space. Members of a composite value are separated by ',' with the key quoted, as canonical JSON.
The id is 'sha256:' followed by the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the canonical text as UTF-8.

cases.name: commas and newlines are whitespace
cases.why: the same shape written by a person and by a generator has one identity

cases.name: each level sorts on its own
an alias is the name a field sorts under
cases.why: the output name is what the caller sees, so it is what identity follows

cases.name: arguments sort by name and are separated by a space
a composite argument value is canonical JSON
cases.shape: { reviews(page: { first: 2, after: "r1" }) { items { rating id } } }
cases.why: quoted keys and commas inside the value, a space between arguments: the two separators are different and both are part of the id

cases.name: a number in an argument takes the form numbers/ pins
cases.why: shape identity inherits the number rule, so 2.50 and 2.5 are one shape

cases.name: a variable reference is kept as written
cases.why: the value is not known when the shape is identified, so the reference itself is what is hashed

cases.name: kinds sort before names: fields, then a type condition, then a defer
@defer takes no key but label
cases.why: the grammar in §1 names label and nothing else. An implementation that reads the key and discards it accepts a shape another rejects, and the two then disagree about which shapes exist at all.

cases.name: @defer's label is a string
cases.why: an implementation that quietly treats a non-string label as absent produces different canonical text for this shape, and so a different id, without anything failing

cases.name: numbers print as ECMAScript prints them
cases.why: the canonical text is what the id hashes, so a runtime that prints 1.0E-4 or 1.23456785E7 (Java's forms) gives the same shape another id, and a trusted-shape list built by one runtime refuses what the other sends

cases.name: a duration is its milliseconds
cases.why: the schema reads 60s as 60000 ms, and a shape argument is read by the same lexer

cases.name: comments are whitespace
cases.shape:
{ id // the key
  title /* shown on the spine */ }
cases.why: a shape kept in a file may carry comments; they are not part of its identity
